title: Sort and Compare
description: Sort fraction cards, each with a pizza, a chocolate bar or a jug beside it, into unit, proper and improper, check whether two cards are like or unlike, and line up like fractions to see which is bigger.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Read the kind of a fraction from its two numbers, tell like from unlike by the bottom numbers, and say which of two like fractions is bigger by comparing the top numbers, with a real pizza, bar or jug beside every card to check the reading.
writeup.look: A tray of fraction cards at the left, each beside a real object cut or filled to show it, two labelled bins at the right, a mat for two cards, and on the last phase two identical objects from one edge and a line-up row.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Sort and Compare' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many cards have been sorted so far, out of the cards on the tray. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The tray of cards stands at the left, its top left at x 80, y 230, six cards in three columns and two rows, each 190 by 150 with 15 between them. A card holds the fraction written large at its left, the top number above a level line above the bottom number, and its real object at its right, 120 across and 100 tall, drawn in natural colours: a pizza cut into slices, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, a plate of laddoos, a row of kites or a round cake. The parts the top number counts sit on a small deep blue plate under the object, labelled Taken, or inside a deep blue ring on a jug, and the parts left stay on the object. An improper card slides a second pizza, bar or cake in beside the first, so one whole and more is drawn, and a card with the same number top and bottom shows exactly one whole object inside a green outline labelled Whole. The two bins stand at the right of the working area, each 200 by 300 with its label on top, at x 700, y 230 and x 920, y 230 on the first two phases. On the third phase the bins give way to the mat at x 700, y 250, 420 by 260, with room for two cards and their two objects side by side and the two bottom numbers lighting amber above it together, and a Like button and an Unlike button under it, each labelled in words. On the fourth phase two identical objects, two chocolate bars 620 long and 100 tall from one common left edge at x 160, y 250 and y 370, or two jugs from one common base, with their equal parts drawn in, stand one above the other, and under them a line-up row of three or four objects with a slot for each place at y 520, smallest first. The object that is tapped as the bigger one gets a vermilion ring and is labelled Bigger. A Check button sits under the bins and the mat, labelled in words, and a Shape view button beside it swaps every real object for a plain strip cut into the same equal parts. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a fraction bar key, for typing a fraction into the answer slot, and the Like and Unlike buttons on the third phase. A card whose bottom number is above ten, such as a sixteenth, is drawn with no picture and is sorted by its two numbers alone. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting it. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, labelled Coloured or Taken, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of the same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket, labelled Left. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, labelled Whole, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring, labelled Bigger. A part of a plain drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its near-black outline, every cut line is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last row of objects stands from the smallest to the biggest, the biggest ringed in vermilion, with each card's fraction written under its object.

phases.win: the unit cards sit in their bin, each object showing a single part on its blue plate
phases.does: reads the top number of each card, drags it to a bin, then taps Check
phases.goal: a fraction with one as its top number is a unit fraction
phases.says: Look at the top number on each card. Which cards have a one on top?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a pizza card has a one on top and a bigger number below. Is it a unit fraction? How many slices are taken?
phases.feels: the cards with one slice, square or mark taken gathering in one bin, however big the pizza or bar was
phases.hands: Draw a pizza, a chocolate bar and a jug on paper, cut each into equal parts, and write the fraction on the back. Sort them into two piles, the ones with one part taken and the rest.
phases.tries: First rung: point to the top number of the card. Second rung: count the slices on the blue plate beside the pizza. Third rung: the same task with only two cards on the tray, before the full tray returns.

wrong.why: the bottom number is the big, easy one to read first
wrong.move: puts a card in the Top number is one bin because of its bottom number
wrong.screen: the object's parts on the blue plate are counted: the taken slices light amber in turn, and the count is written beside the top number

wrong.why: a pizza with many slices looks like a lot of fraction
wrong.move: leaves a card with one slice taken out of the bin, because the pizza has many slices
wrong.screen: the pizza's other slices dim to half strength, so the single slice on the blue plate stands alone beside the one on top

phases.screen: a tray of six cards, each with its pizza, bar, jug, cake, laddoos or kites, and two empty bins, Top number is one and Not one
phases.soWhat: a unit fraction has one as its top number
phases.concept: Unit fractions: the top number is one

phases.win: an improper card shows one whole pizza on the blue plate and more slices from a second pizza
phases.does: reads both numbers of a card, drags it to a bin, and watches the pizzas and bars
phases.goal: a fraction is proper when its top is smaller than its bottom, and improper when it is bigger or the same
phases.says: Is the top number smaller than the bottom number? Look at the pictures too.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a cake card has a smaller number on top than on the bottom. Is it more than one whole cake, or less?
phases.feels: a second pizza sliding in beside a card exactly when its top number gets past the bottom
phases.hands: Use paper pizzas cut into equal slices. Put more slices on a plate than one pizza holds, cut a second paper pizza, and say whether the top number or the bottom number is bigger.
phases.tries: First rung: read the top number, then the bottom number. Second rung: look at whether the first pizza is full. Third rung: the same task with a card whose top number is only one more than its bottom number.

wrong.why: a big number feels like a lot, and a lot feels like more than one
wrong.move: calls a card proper because its top number is a big number
wrong.screen: the two numbers are set side by side and the slices on the plate are counted, and a second pizza slides in only where the first pizza is full

wrong.why: it is only one pizza, so it does not look like more than one whole
wrong.move: calls a card with the same number top and bottom proper
wrong.screen: the whole pizza is ringed in green and labelled Whole, with the words top number the same as bottom number beside it

phases.screen: a tray of cards and two bins, Proper and Improper, with a second pizza, bar or cake beside any card that needs one
phases.soWhat: a proper fraction has a top number smaller than its bottom number, and an improper fraction has a top number bigger than or the same as its bottom number
phases.concept: Proper and improper: is the top number smaller?

phases.win: the two bottom numbers light together, the two objects show parts of one size, and the mat reads Like
phases.does: puts two cards on the mat, reads the lit bottom numbers, and taps Like or Unlike
phases.goal: fractions with the same bottom number are like, and fractions with different bottom numbers are unlike
phases.says: Put two cards on the mat. Do the two bottom numbers match?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two jug cards have different top numbers and the same bottom number. Are they like or unlike?
phases.feels: the two bottom numbers lighting up together on the mat, and the top numbers staying quiet
phases.hands: Write six fractions on cards, each beside a drawn pizza or bar. Lay two on the desk and cover their top numbers with a finger, so only the bottom numbers can be read. Say like or unlike.
phases.tries: First rung: cover the top numbers. Second rung: say the two bottom numbers aloud. Third rung: the same task with a pair whose bottom numbers are one apart.

wrong.why: the matching numbers are the first thing the eye catches
wrong.move: says like because the two top numbers are the same
wrong.screen: the two bottom numbers light amber together and the top numbers dim to half strength, and the two objects show parts of different sizes

wrong.why: different amounts taken feel like different fractions
wrong.move: says unlike because the two cards show different amounts taken
wrong.screen: the two objects are shown cut into the same number of equal parts, with the bottom number lit on both, and the words same bottom number appear beside them

phases.screen: a mat with room for two cards and their two objects, and a pair of cards waiting beside it
phases.soWhat: fractions with the same bottom number are like fractions, and fractions with different bottom numbers are unlike
phases.concept: Like and unlike: do the bottom numbers match?

phases.win: the bigger one gets a vermilion ring and is labelled Bigger
phases.does: taps the object with more parts taken, then drags objects into a row from the smallest to the biggest
phases.goal: between two like fractions the one with the bigger top number is bigger
phases.says: The parts are the same size. Which one has more parts taken?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two like jug cards have top numbers three and five. Which jug has more juice, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the longer taken stretch getting its vermilion ring, with all the parts the same size
phases.hands: Draw chocolate bars of ten squares, eat a different number of squares on each, and line them up from one left edge. Say which bar has the most eaten and write each fraction.
phases.tries: First rung: check that the two objects have the same number of equal parts. Second rung: count the parts taken from each. Third rung: the same task with the taken parts counted aloud while they light up in turn.

wrong.why: the bottom number is the big number on the card, so it feels like the one that counts
wrong.move: says the bar with the bigger bottom number is bigger, when the bottom numbers match
wrong.screen: both bottom numbers light amber as the same number, and the squares are counted by the ones taken, the longer taken stretch glowing

wrong.why: two fractions on one screen look as if they can always be compared
wrong.move: tries to compare two cards that have different bottom numbers
wrong.screen: the mat says in words that fractions with different bottom numbers need more steps that are not met yet, and offers a pair of like cards

wrong.why: the biggest one catches the eye and goes first
wrong.move: lines the objects up from the biggest
wrong.screen: the first slot is marked Smallest in words, and the object placed there is checked against the object beside it

phases.screen: two identical objects cut into equal parts, side by side from one common edge, and a line-up row
phases.soWhat: between two like fractions, the one with the bigger top number is bigger

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the line-up row is finished in the right order, the chocolate bars slide together into one staircase, each step one square longer than the one before, and the biggest gets its vermilion ring. On any jug card, the juice rises one mark at a time to the top number as the card is picked up.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing sorted yet. On the first phase the tray holds six cards, each with its pizza, chocolate bar, jug, cake, plate of laddoos or row of kites, and the two bins Top number is one and Not one stand empty at the right. On the second the bins are Proper and Improper, and the improper cards already have their second pizza, bar or cake beside the first. On the third the mat is empty and a pair of cards waits beside it. On the fourth two identical objects stand side by side from one common edge. One thing moves, once: the first card, or the first object on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any cards sorted into any bins, any two cards on the mat, two identical objects stood from one edge and a row of objects lined up. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, each with a pizza, a chocolate bar, a jug, a cake, laddoos or kites: unit cards, proper and improper cards, like and unlike pairs, and the bigger of two like fractions.
voiceLines: Some fraction cards, and a real thing beside each one.
Look at the top number on each card. Which cards have a one on top?
Is the top number smaller than the bottom number? Look at the pictures too.
Put two cards on the mat. Do the two bottom numbers match?
The parts are the same size. Which one has more parts taken?
A new set of cards. Read the numbers before you drop one.
Free play. Sort, match and line up the pizzas and bars as you like.
Look at the picture again. Count the parts on the plate, then all the parts.
You told the kinds apart by reading the top and bottom numbers.

observations.why: the top number counts the parts taken, and a unit fraction has exactly one of them.
observations.soWhat: a unit fraction has one as its top number.
observations.observe: A card with a one on top showed a single slice, square or mark on the blue plate, however many parts the pizza or bar had.

observations.why: one pizza holds only as many slices as its bottom number, so more slices on the plate need a second pizza.
observations.soWhat: an improper fraction is one whole or more, and its top number is bigger than or the same as its bottom number.
observations.observe: A card whose top number was bigger than its bottom number slid a second pizza in beside the first.

observations.why: like and unlike are about the size of the parts, which the bottom number gives, and not about how many are taken.
observations.soWhat: fractions with the same bottom number are like, whatever their top numbers are.
observations.observe: The mat lit the two bottom numbers together, and the top numbers stayed dark.

observations.why: the two bars were cut into the same number of equal squares, so more squares taken is a longer taken stretch.
observations.soWhat: between two like fractions, the one with the bigger top number is bigger.
observations.observe: The chocolate bar with more squares taken reached further from the left edge, and the squares were all the same size.

phases.screen: a tray of six cards, each with its pizza, bar, jug, cake, laddoos or kites, and two empty bins, Top number is one and Not one
phases.win: the unit cards sit in their bin, each object showing a single part on its blue plate
phases.traceback: Each card's top number lights amber in turn, then the right cards show dashed in the bin.
ladder: Point to the top number of the card.
Check the top number, not the bottom one.
Find the card with a number other than 1 on top.

phases.screen: a tray of cards and two bins, Proper and Improper, with a second pizza, bar or cake beside any card that needs one
phases.win: an improper card shows one whole pizza on the blue plate and more slices from a second pizza
phases.traceback: The top and bottom numbers light amber, then the right answer key is ringed green, or the right cards show dashed in the bin.
ladder: Look at whether the first pizza is full.
Read the top number, then the bottom number.
Read both numbers on every card before you sort it.

phases.screen: a mat with room for two cards and their two objects, and a pair of cards waiting beside it
phases.win: the two bottom numbers light together, the two objects show parts of one size, and the mat reads Like
phases.traceback: The bottom numbers light amber together and the top numbers fade, then the right answer key is ringed green, or the right cards show dashed in the bin.
ladder: Cover the top numbers.
Do the two bottom numbers match?
Read the bottom number on each card.

phases.screen: two identical objects cut into equal parts, side by side from one common edge, and a line-up row
phases.win: the bigger one gets a vermilion ring and is labelled Bigger
phases.traceback: The bigger whole gets the vermilion Bigger ring, or an equals sign when they match, and the right answer key is ringed green.
ladder: The squares are all the same size.
Different bottom numbers: look at the pictures, the numbers cannot tell us yet.
Compare the blue part of each pizza, not the numbers.
Both chocolate bars have 10 equal squares, so count the blue squares.
More blue squares of the same size reach further along the chocolate bar.
How many blue squares are taken from the chocolate bar?
A unit fraction takes just 1 part, however many parts the whole has.
items.win: Yes, 1/10 has 1 on top, so it is a unit fraction.

ladder: Say the top number of each card out loud.
Only cards with 1 above the line belong in this bin.
items.win: Right, 1/5 and 1/9 both have 1 on top.

ladder: Look at the blue parts: which card has more than 1 taken?
Three cards have 1 on top; move the card whose top is different.
items.win: Right, 2/9 has 2 on top, so it is not a unit fraction.

ladder: Is 7 smaller than 4, or bigger?
The top counts the slices taken; the bottom counts the slices in one pizza.
items.win: Yes, 7 is bigger than 4, so 7/4 is more than one pizza.

ladder: Is 8 smaller than 9, or bigger?
Count the pieces left: is any of the roti still there?
items.win: Yes, 8 is smaller than 9, so 8/9 is less than one roti.

ladder: A card with the same top and bottom number shows one whole.
Improper means the top number is bigger than the bottom, or the same.
items.win: Right, 9/5 is more than one whole and 8/8 is one whole, so both are improper.

ladder: Say the two bottom numbers aloud.
Like cards share one bottom number, whatever their top numbers are.
items.win: Yes, 5 and 9 are different, so 4/5 and 4/9 are unlike.

ladder: Forget the blue parts and read the numbers under the lines.
Are both rotis cut into the same number of pieces?
items.win: Yes, both bottom numbers are 9, so they are like.

ladder: Which bottom number do three cards share?
Find the card whose bottom number is different from the rest.
items.win: Right, 4/7 is the only card without 9 at the bottom.
Yes, 6/10 is smaller, because 6 squares are fewer than 9.

ladder: Which roti has more of its round covered in blue?
Trace each blue part with a finger and see which one is wider.
items.win: Yes, half a roti is more than a quarter of the same roti.

ladder: Does one blue part cover more of its pizza than the other?
Picture one pizza laid on the other: which blue part is wider?
items.win: Yes, 2/4 of a pizza covers the same as 1/2 of it.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Each card's top number lights amber in turn, then the right cards show dashed in the bin.
Phase 2: The top and bottom numbers light amber, then the right answer key is ringed green, or the right cards show dashed in the bin.
Phase 3: The bottom numbers light amber together and the top numbers fade, then the right answer key is ringed green, or the right cards show dashed in the bin.
Phase 4: The bigger whole gets the vermilion Bigger ring, or an equals sign when they match, and the right answer key is ringed green.

voice.opening: Some fraction cards, and a real thing beside each one.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: tap the cards into the bin and back as you like.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: You told the kinds apart by reading the top and bottom numbers.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.
guide.answerGate: Sort questions (pad 'enter': phase 1 questions 2-3, phase 2 question 3, phase 3 question 3): in user mode, once a real finger or mouse has touched the board, the Enter key is disabled (flat, untappable, no blink) until the child moves a card in that question; the agent's toolApi path is never gated. The word-key questions (Yes/No, Proper/Improper, Like/Unlike, Greater/Smaller/Equal) have no act and are never gated.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A chocolate bar has 10 equal squares and 1 square is eaten. The card says 1/10. Is it a unit fraction? How do you know?

question.en: A chocolate bar of 10 equal squares has some eaten: is this a unit fraction?

items.planAnswer: Yes, because the top number is one

items.planQuestion: The tray holds a pizza card 1/5, a chocolate bar card 2/5, a jug card 1/9 and a cake card 6/9. Which cards go in the bin Top number is one?

question.en: Tap every unit fraction card into the bin, then press Enter.

items.planAnswer: The pizza card 1/5 and the jug card 1/9

items.planQuestion: The tray holds a pizza card 1/3, a kite row card 1/7, a cake card 2/9 and a jug card 1/10. Which card is not a unit fraction?

question.en: Now put the one card that is not a unit fraction in the bin.

items.planAnswer: The cake card 2/9, because its top number is two and not one

items.planQuestion: A pizza card shows 7/4, and every pizza is cut into 4 slices. Is 7/4 proper or improper? Use the pizzas to see.

question.en: Every pizza is cut into 4 slices: is 7/4 proper or improper?

items.planQuestion: A round cake is cut into 9 equal slices and 8 slices are eaten. The card says 8/9. Is it proper or improper?

question.en: A roti cut into 9 equal pieces has 8 eaten: which kind is 8/9?

items.planAnswer: Proper, because 8 is smaller than 9, so it is less than one whole cake

items.planQuestion: The tray holds a pizza card 9/5, a chocolate bar card 5/8, a cake card 8/8 and a jug card 2/9. Which cards are improper?

question.en: Tap every improper card into the bin, then press Enter.

items.planAnswer: The pizza card 9/5 and the cake card 8/8, because their top numbers are bigger than or the same as their bottom numbers

items.planQuestion: The mat holds a pizza card 4/5 and a chocolate bar card 4/9. Are the two cards like or unlike?

question.en: The mat holds 4/5 and 4/9: are the two cards like or unlike?

items.planQuestion: Two plates each hold 9 laddoos. On one plate 1 laddoo is taken and on the other plate 7 are taken. The cards say 1/9 and 7/9. Are they like or unlike?

question.en: One roti has 1 piece taken, the other has 7: what kind of pair is it?

items.planAnswer: Like, because both bottom numbers are 9

items.planQuestion: Four cards wait on the tray: a laddoo plate 2/9, a pizza 5/9, a chocolate bar 4/9 and a kite row 4/7. Which card is the odd one out?

question.en: One card is not like the others: put it in the bin, then press Enter.

items.planAnswer: The kite row 4/7, because the other three have 9 as the bottom number, so they are like fractions

items.planQuestion: Two chocolate bars of the same size each have ten squares. One has 6 squares eaten and the other has 9. Which fraction is bigger?

question.en: Is 6/10 of a chocolate bar greater than, smaller than or equal to 9/10 of it?
The two rotis are the same size: how does 1/2 compare with 1/4?
One pizza is cut into 2 and its twin into 4: how does 1/2 compare with 2/4?

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: Unit fractions: the top number is one
Proper and improper: is the top number smaller?
Like and unlike: do the bottom numbers match?

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), inBin, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves

voiceLines.en: Some fraction cards, and a real thing beside each one.
Look at the top number on each card. Which cards have a one on top?
Is the top number smaller than the bottom number? Look at the pictures too.
Put two cards on the mat. Do the two bottom numbers match?
The parts are the same size. Which one has more parts taken?
A new set of cards. Read the numbers before you drop one.
Free play. Sort, match and line up the pizzas and bars as you like.
Look at the picture again. Count the parts on the plate, then all the parts.
You told the kinds apart by reading the top and bottom numbers.
